items.title: John Levy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Cannonball and Joe Williams were the two people – the two main people that were my friends. ... We loved each other like brothers.

ctx.x: You had mentioned there was something unique about her style of speech, her . . .

Dinah Washington was, in my estimation, the most articulate vocalist of any time. She sang – each syllable was so perfect, and her diction was such that it was just amazing. You [don’t] figure someone from the South or black, especially at that time period, to speak like Dinah did. Her diction was perfect. Her English was just perfect. The only other person that I think he learned from her, was Joe Williams, because they worked together with Lionel Hampton’s. From that – they worked together as the singer – the…
Joe Williams was playing around that time at the Sherman Hotel and . . .

items.title: John Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995
items.q: I knew Joe, for years I’d known Joe Williams... he called me one day he said, 'come and take this telephone out of my hands.'... I work with because he’s with Joe and anything I can do to work with him is fine

ctx.x: And like what was the status—

That was the time when Basie finally broke up and had the six pieces, you know, because it was really rough out there for big bands. But groups like George was really hot, and Dave Brubeck, and that was the hottest things going, playing the colleges and you know, so it was really — the big band it just cost too much to travel. And the economics of it at that time was even worse than they are now. I mean they’re bad enough now, but for a big band it was terrible, you know. But anyway, that’s how I got into that…

business. And then one by one different people came along. And I knew Joe, for years I’d known Joe Williams. And when he left the Basie band and he called me one day he said, “come and take this telephone out of my hands.”
